en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 40, the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅgas at a market town of the Aṅgas named Assapura.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“‘Ascetics, ascetics,’ bhikkhus, is how people perceive you.”
And when you are asked, ‘Who are you?’, you claim, ‘We are ascetics. Now, monks, for you who have such a designation and such a profession, [you should think]:
‘We shall practice that which is the proper way of conduct for an ascetic.’
In this way, our designation will be true and our promise will be factual;
and for those from whom we enjoy robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
their services toward us will become highly fruitful and of great benefit, and this very going-forth of ours [will have been well-taken].
"It will not be barren; it will be fruitful and productive.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
And how, monks, does a monk fail to practice the way of conduct befitting a recluse?
“Monks, for any monk whatsoever who is covetous, covetousness has not been abandoned; who is malevolent in mind, ill will has not been abandoned;
who is angry, anger has not been abandoned; who is resentful, resentment has not been abandoned;
who is contemptuous, contempt has not been abandoned; who is spiteful, spite has not been abandoned; who is envious, envy has not been abandoned.”
For one who is stingy, stinginess has not been abandoned; for one who is deceitful, deceitfulness has not been abandoned;
for one who is fraudulent, fraudulence has not been abandoned; for one who has evil desires, evil desire has not been abandoned;
for one who holds wrong view, wrong view has not been abandoned.

“Bhikkhus, I say that because one has not abandoned these stains of ascetics, faults of ascetics, and impurities of ascetics—which lead to states of deprivation and result in rebirth in miserable destinations—one has not entered upon the practice that accords with the dignity of an ascetic.
It is just as if there were a kind of weapon called a *mataja*, double-edged and whetted on both sides;
yet it were wrapped and enveloped in an outer robe.”
“Monks, I say that this bhikkhu’s going forth is just like that.
Monks, I do not say that one who wears a robe has the state of a recluse merely by wearing a robe.
Monks, I do not say that one who is naked has the state of a recluse merely by being naked.”
“Monks, I do not say that one who wears dust and dirt becomes an ascetic by the mere wearing of dust and dirt.
Monks, I do not say that one who bathes in water becomes an ascetic by the mere bathing in water.
Monks, I do not say that one who dwells at the root of a tree becomes an ascetic by the mere dwelling at the root of a tree.”
“Monks, I do not say that one who lives in the open air has the quality of a recluse merely by living in the open air.
Monks, I do not say that one who stands continuously has the quality of a recluse merely by standing continuously.
Monks, I do not say that one who eats at fixed intervals has the quality of a recluse merely by eating at fixed intervals.”
“Monks, I do not say that one who studies the mantras attains the state of a recluse merely by being a student of the mantras.
Nor, monks, do I say that one with matted hair attains the state of a recluse merely by wearing matted hair.
If, monks, for one who wears the outer robe, the state of a recluse were attained merely by wearing the outer robe, then the covetousness of a covetous person would be abandoned.”
In one with a malicious mind, malice would be abandoned; in one who is angry, anger would be abandoned; in one who harbors resentment, resentment would be abandoned;
in one who is contemptuous, contempt would be abandoned; in one who is spiteful, spite would be abandoned; in one who is envious, envy would be abandoned;
in one who is stingy, stinginess would be abandoned; in one who is deceitful, deceitfulness would be abandoned; in one who is fraudulent...
Illusion would be abandoned; the evil desire of one with evil desires would be abandoned; the wrong view of one with wrong views would be abandoned.

Then his friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would, as soon as he was born, make him a wearer of the patched robe (*saṅghāṭika*) and would encourage him toward the state of being a wearer of the patched robe, saying:
“Come, good sir, be a wearer of the patched robe! For you who are a wearer of the patched robe, by the mere wearing of the patched robe...”
For one who is covetous, covetousness will be abandoned; for one with a mind of ill will, ill will will be abandoned;
for one who is angry, anger will be abandoned; for one who is resentful, resentment will be abandoned; for one who is contemptuous, contempt will be abandoned;
for one who is spiteful, spite will be abandoned; for one who is envious, envy will be abandoned; for one who is miserly, miserliness will be abandoned.
‘The craftiness of the crafty will be abandoned; the deceit of the deceitful will be abandoned; the guile of the guileful will be abandoned;
the evil desire of the one with evil desires will be abandoned; the wrong view of the one with wrong view will be abandoned.
Yet, monks, because I see here some who, even though they wear the outer robe of the Saṅgha, are covetous and possess minds of ill will...”

One who is angry, resentful, hypocritical, spiteful, envious, stingy, fraudulent, deceitful, of evil desires, and of wrong view—therefore, I do not say that one possesses the state of a recluse merely by wearing the outer robe of a monk.
Even if one is naked, monks... [and so forth].

If, monks, [a bhikkhu] is one who dwells in the open air …pe… if,
monks, [a bhikkhu] is one who remains standing …pe… if,
monks, [a bhikkhu] is one who takes food at intervals …pe…

“Monks, if for a reciter of mantras …pe… or for a matted-hair ascetic, monks, by the mere wearing of matted hair, covetousness were abandoned in one who is covetous; ill will were abandoned in one with a mind of ill will;
anger were abandoned in one who is angry; resentment were abandoned in one who is resentful; and disparagement were abandoned in one who is disparaging…”
Deceit would be abandoned; in one who is spiteful, spite would be abandoned; in one who is envious, envy would be abandoned; in one who is stingy, stinginess would be abandoned;
in one who is fraudulent, fraud would be abandoned; in one who is deceitful, deceit would be abandoned;
in one who has evil desires, evil desire would be abandoned; in one who holds wrong view, wrong view would be abandoned. Then his friends and companions—
His kinsmen and blood relatives would have him become a matted-hair ascetic as soon as he was born; they would urge him toward the very state of a matted-hair ascetic, saying:

"Come, dear child, be a matted-hair ascetic! For you, being a matted-hair ascetic, by the mere wearing of matted hair, covetousness will be abandoned in one who is covetous, ill-will will be abandoned in one with a mind of malice, and anger will be abandoned in one who is angry."
"...pe... 'the evil desire of one with evil desires will be abandoned; the wrong view of one with wrong view will be abandoned.

Yet, monks, because I see here some of those with matted hair who are covetous, of ill-will, angry, resentful, contemptuous, slanderous, envious, miserly, fraudulent, deceitful, of evil desires, and of wrong view,"
Therefore, I do not say that a matted-hair ascetic possesses the state of a recluse merely by wearing matted hair.
And how, monks, does a monk practice the way of conduct befitting a recluse?
Monks, when whatever covetousness a monk may have is abandoned, and whatever ill will he may have in his heart...
Ill will has been abandoned; the anger of one prone to anger has been abandoned; the resentment of one prone to resentment has been abandoned;
the disparagement of one prone to disparagement has been abandoned; the spite of one prone to spite has been abandoned; the envy of one prone to envy has been abandoned;
the stinginess of one prone to stinginess has been abandoned; the deceitfulness of one prone to deceit has been abandoned; the guile of one prone to guile has been abandoned.
Deceit has been abandoned; the evil desires of one with evil wishes have been abandoned; the wrong view of one with wrong view has been abandoned.

It is, monks, because of the abandoning of these stains of ascetics, these faults of ascetics, these impurities of ascetics—which lead to states of deprivation and result in rebirth in miserable destinies—that I say of one: "He has entered upon the practice that accords with the proper conduct of an ascetic.
He regards himself as purified of all these evil, unwholesome states. (...)
As he perceives himself as purified of all these evil, unwholesome states, gladness arises;
in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness;
and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
Thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind accompanied by compassion …pe… with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… with a mind accompanied by equanimity,
he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, [likewise the fourth].

And so it is with the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Monks, it is just as if there were a lotus pond with clear water, sweet water, cool water, white water, with good landing places, and delightful.

If a man should come from the eastern direction, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, weary, thirsty, and parched with thirst, and having reached that lotus pond, he should dispel his thirst for water and dispel the fever of the heat... [and] if a man should come from the western direction...
[and] if a man should come from the northern direction... [and] if a man should come from the southern direction.
Suppose a man were to come from any direction whatsoever— perhaps from somewhere or other—
oppressed by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty; having reached that lotus pond,
he would dispel his thirst for water and dispel the fever of the heat.
In the same way, monks, if one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a khattiya family,
having relied upon the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, develops loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity,
he attains internal tranquility. From internal tranquility comes the practice that accords with the conduct of a recluse.
I say that he is one who is practicing rightly. Whether it be from a brahmin family, or from a merchant family, or from a worker family,
or from whatever family he may have gone forth from the home life into homelessness,
if he— relying on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata— develops loving-kindness, compassion, gladness, and equanimity in this way, he attains internal tranquility.
I say that one who has attained internal tranquility is practicing the way of conduct befitting a recluse.
Even if one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from a kshatriya family, and having,

through the destruction of the taints, realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells therein.
Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse. Whether from a brahmin family, or from a merchant family, or from a worker family,
or from whatever family he may have gone forth from the home life into homelessness— if, through the destruction of the taints,
he has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it and remained therein— then he is a recluse.
He dwells [thus]. Through the destruction of the taints, he becomes a true ascetic.
This is what the Blessed One said.
With uplifted minds, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Cūḷa-assapura Sutta, the tenth, is finished.
The fourth chapter, the Mahāyamaka Vagga, is finished.
Here is its summary verse:
To maintain the Giñjakasālavana monastery,
there was the further refutation of Saccaka by the wise one;
[and] the alms-food from the brightening of his facial expression.
By the matted-hair ascetic of Kevaṭṭa’s town.
